newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists in 100 bln Ffr budget proposals.
newsitem.headline: French Communists in 100 bln Ffr budget proposals.

text.p: France's Communist Party waded into debate over the 1998 budget on Monday with a 100 billion franc ($16.3 billion) programme to promote economic growth.

The Communist plan includes taxing capital flows, a mandatory loan to the government from banks and insurance companies to pay the country's debt service, financial aid to local authorities so they can create jobs, higher employer charges and higher income taxes for the wealthiest.
It also includes proposals for cutting income tax for all but the wealthiest families, lowering sales tax on essential items and cutting the electricity, housing and other taxes.

The Communists, junior partners in the Socialist-led government of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin, said their project would produce about 100 billion francs in new receipts, matching the planned spending to relaunch the economy.

The party's budget proposals are unlikely to enter the final 1998 finance act. Jospin set the government's spending targets on August 8 and is expected to begin wrestling with the revenue side of the budget this week.
The party said the plan would not hurt the government's deficit cutting, which it acknowledged as an important goal.

"These measures could be financed with no rise in the deficit," the Communists' open letter to Jospin said. "On the contrary, the fiscal receipts from the (economic) rebound and the reduction in spending...can lead to the reduction of the deficit in 1998."
The Communists control two ministries in Jospin's government which came to power in June after ousting the former conservative coalition in an upset election.
In an open letter to Jospin, the Communists said budgets of the "priority" ministries should rise significantly.

These ministries include education, training, research, health, youth and sports, culture and housing, the letter, from Alain Bocquet, leader of the Communist Party's National Assembly delegation, said.
"A particular effort for industry and public companies is decisive to restart the French economy," Bocquet's letter said.

The letter went on to say that small and medium-sized companies, seen as the potential engine of employment growth, could benefit from raising a limit on home savings accounts that are used to give corporate loans.
The Communist plan calls for taxes on income from savings and investment to be equal to taxes on work. It also proposed a lower level of corporate tax on profits that are reinvested to create jobs.

Corporate tax would be raised, however, on any profitable company that enacted economic redundancy programmes and that company would not be able to use government jobs subsidies to hire workers for two years.
The plan also includes doubling income from the wealth tax by including professional assets and works of art when wealth is calculated.
